title: Using Digital Technology to Improve Learning: Evidence Review
extended_summary:
This report is an evidence review of how digital technology has been used to improve learning outcomes, focusing on whether technology is effective when compared with conventional instruction and other non-digital approaches. The review updates earlier synthesis work and examines more recent meta-analyses, systematic reviews, and selected English school studies published since 2012.

The paper organizes the evidence by subject domain (literacy/language, mathematics, science) and by pedagogical use (for example, learning from experts, learning through practice, exploring through simulations and games, and learning across settings through mobile technology). It includes studies from school-age populations, mainly primary and secondary learners, but also some studies with adults in mixed samples. Across the literature, the comparison condition is typically traditional classroom practice, regular classroom instruction, or non-technology alternatives such as teacher-led teaching, paper-based materials, or no-treatment controls.

Overall, the review concludes that digital technology usually has small to moderate positive effects when used as a supplement to normal teaching rather than as a replacement for it. Stronger effects are often seen when technology provides structured practice, adaptive scaffolding, simulations, or intelligent tutoring, while results are weaker or inconsistent for some reading and general technology applications. The review also emphasizes that pedagogy, implementation, and teacher professional development matter more than the technology itself.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-review/evidence review synthesizing multiple meta-analyses and selected high-quality studies, with explicit attention to study design, AMSTAR2, and GRADE. It therefore meets the highest evidence-synthesis standard in the provided framework, despite heterogeneity and some low-certainty sub-analyses.
impact_tier_rationale: The review reports many effect sizes at or above 0.20, including several moderate effects for simulations, scaffolding, mobile learning, and some literacy and math interventions. Although impacts vary by intervention and comparator, the overall literature synthesis indicates meaningful positive effects in several priority domains.

interventions.use_case: Evidence review of software-delivered instruction that provides additional or supplemental instruction at students' assessed levels of need, often through drill-and-practice programs, compared with regular classroom instruction or no treatment.
Review of adaptive, interactive tutoring systems that respond to learner actions and provide scaffolding or guided feedback, compared with conventional instruction.
Review of game-based learning, serious games, simulations, and exploratory computerized environments used for literacy, mathematics, science, and language learning.
Review of mobile learning applications and mobile-supported learning across settings, including language learning and inquiry-based learning.
Review of automated, adapted guidance systems and enhanced automatic guidance that personalize support based on learner performance.

finding.finding_summary: Across literacy and language studies, technology generally produced small positive effects versus traditional classroom practice, but results varied by intervention and outcome. For example, ABRACADABRA improved phonics (0.189), phonemic awareness (0.324), listening comprehension (0.381), and vocabulary (0.138), but showed no effect on reading fluency or comprehension; a later EEF study found literacy gains of 0.138, while an offline equivalent performed better at 0.231.
finding.measure: Reading, phonics, phonemic awareness, listening comprehension, vocabulary, reading fluency, reading comprehension, literacy scores
finding.effect_size: 0.138 to 0.381 (reported by outcome); 0.138 vs 0.231 in EEF comparison

finding.finding_summary: Technology generally had a positive effect on second-language learning, especially when used for mobile learning or computer-mediated communication. Reported effects ranged from 0.29 to 0.873 overall, with specific gains such as 0.837 for mobile learning in second/foreign language learning and 0.610 for computer-mediated communication in foreign language learning.
finding.measure: Second-language learning, language learning achievement, communication-based language learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The mathematics literature was broadly positive, with small-to-moderate effects for several technology uses relative to conventional instruction. Reported effects included 0.16 for CAI, 0.49 for simulations, 0.60 for exploratory computerized environments, 0.44 for ITS, and 0.65 in some subgroup estimates; one meta-analysis found no overall effect for adjusted ITS estimates (g=0.01).
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement, algebra, numeracy, problem solving
finding.effect_size: 0.01 to 0.65; one estimate 0.44 for ITS, 0.49 for simulations, 0.16 for CAI

finding.finding_summary: Science outcomes were generally positive, especially for simulations and mobile/inquiry-based learning. Reported effects included 0.62 overall for simulations in science, 0.82 for primary science in one review (with some estimates based on very few studies), 0.91 for mobile learning/inquiry-based learning, and smaller positive effects for one-to-one laptop programs.
finding.measure: Science achievement, inquiry-based science learning, science and technology outcomes

finding.finding_summary: Some reviewed interventions also improved engagement-like or motivational outcomes, especially when games or structured digital supports were used, though the report mainly centered attainment. For serious games and game-based learning, the review notes benefits for skills and in-game performance, suggesting potential support for persistence and engagement, but these were not the primary outcomes and were not consistently quantified.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, in-game performance, skills-related outcomes

finding.finding_summary: Digital tools that supported scaffolding, inquiry, and exploratory learning were associated with gains in higher-order skills such as problem solving and metacognition. For example, game-based learning with instructional support outperformed games without support (0.34), and teacher-provided scaffolding in games was especially effective (0.58); one STEM scaffolding review also reported stronger effects for metacognitive and strategic scaffolding than conceptual scaffolding.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem solving, metacognition, strategic learning skills
finding.effect_size: 0.34 to 0.58 for supported games; g=0.384 and g=0.345 for metacognitive/strategic scaffolding in one review

finding.finding_summary: The report argues that digital technology can make teaching and learning more efficient and can provide supplementary practice, but the evidence is mostly indirect rather than based on dedicated workload measures. Conventional classroom instruction was often supplemented by technology that delivered practice or automated guidance, implying efficiency gains, though the review does not report a pooled effect size for teacher workload or time savings.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, instructional efficiency, supplementary practice time
